# Following the scar over thirty days {#sec-longitudinal-timeseries}















Twice in this book I told you that I would come back to something. In @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous I cut the time axis down to days 3 to 14 so that a straight line was defensible, and I said that this was a decision I made after looking at the means, not a law of ischemia. In @sec-linear-models-reflection I said that the bump followed by a plateau, the shape that forced the cut, was a job for a model that bends. This chapter keeps both promises. The question is the one a reviewer would ask of a paper on the glial scar, and the one a postdoc would ask over coffee: **what did the scar do between the day of the lesion and day 30, when did it rise, when did it fall, and how sure are we?**

There is a second promise, made across several chapters. The open-field mice were tested on six days; the neurological score of the mice was recorded on three; the hanging wire on three. I treated those days as if they were interchangeable pieces of evidence and told you each time that this was false in the way that time makes it false. A day is not a replicate of the day before: it comes after it, and an animal that was slow yesterday tends to be slow today. So the chapter has two halves that look similar and are not. In the first, time is a comparison *between* animals and the model needs a **curve**. In the second, time is something that happens *within* animals and the model needs a curve **and** a way of describing how an animal's days resemble each other. The difference between them is the first lesson, and I want to state it before any model. @fig-lt-designs states it in one picture.

On the right, one animal photographed on five days: the change is its own, and the pictures belong together.](images/longitudinal-timeseries_one-day-each-vs-five-days.png){#fig-lt-designs fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch in two halves separated by a faint vertical line. On the left, five different white mice in a row, each beside its own small blank desk calendar. On the right, one white mouse drawn five times along a rising path, each copy beside a blank calendar, joined by a thin teal line with dots."}

## The whole course, with every animal in it {#sec-lt-hook}

The histology data are the ones we have used since @sec-linear-regression-what, in the version of @sec-eda-data-quality: one row per animal, with the area of the section (`Tissue_Area`, in mm²), the number of PDGFR-β+ cells (`Pdgfrb_Pos`) and the integrated density of GFAP (`Gfap_IntDen`). Before any model, I want you to look at all of it at once, with every animal as a point, because a summary of five means can look like a story that five clouds of points do not tell (@fig-lt_hook). The dots are `ggplot2::geom_jitter()` with a little horizontal spread so that animals of the same day do not sit on top of each other, the black line joins the mean of each day, and the shaded band is the window of days 3 to 14 that @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous used.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One long table with the three outcomes, so that one ggplot call draws the three panels
hook <- rbind(
  data.frame(cell_data[, c("MouseID", "DPI", "Condition")], value = cell_data$Tissue_Area, outcome = "Tissue area (mm²)"),
  data.frame(cell_data[, c("MouseID", "DPI", "Condition")], value = cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos, outcome = "PDGFR-β+ cells"),
  data.frame(cell_data[, c("MouseID", "DPI", "Condition")], value = cell_data$Gfap_IntDen, outcome = "GFAP integrated density")
)
hook$outcome <- factor(hook$outcome, levels = c("Tissue area (mm²)", "PDGFR-β+ cells", "GFAP integrated density"))

# Points for every animal, the line through the day means, and the window line extended over the whole range
ggplot(hook, aes(x = DPI, y = value)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 3, xmax = 14, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(data = hook[hook$DPI >= 3 & hook$DPI <= 14, ], method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              fullrange = TRUE, color = "grey30", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Condition, shape = Condition), width = 0.7, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 0.9) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_cond) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days after the lesion (DPI)", y = NULL, color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()
```

Showing every animal is not decoration. A bar plot with asterisks would give you five bars and a verdict, and it would hide the three things that matter in @fig-lt_hook: that the tissue area of day 3 is the most spread of all days, that the counts of PDGFR-β+ cells jump between days 3 and 7 and not gradually, and that the GFAP points of day 30 are not one cloud but two (which I come back to). The black line joining the day means is a way of seeing, not a model: it joins five numbers and says nothing about what happens between them.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read each panel from left to right as if it were a film, and ask three things in this order. First, where is the rise and where is the fall: for the tissue area the mean goes up at day 3 and then down, for the PDGFR-β+ counts it jumps between days 3 and 7 and eases off at day 30, for GFAP it rises until day 14 and falls back. Second, where is the spread large: it differs from day to day and from marker to marker, and a single `sigma` would not describe it. Third, compare the dashed line with the means outside the shaded band. The line was fitted only inside the band, so it is a fair summary of days 3 to 14 and a poor guide to what happens outside it: in the first panel it runs below zero tissue area before day 30, in the second and third it overshoots the animals of day 30 by a wide margin. The mistake to avoid is joining the means and calling it a curve: five points do not tell you what happens on day 5 or day 20.
:::

Two facts about the design of these data shape everything that follows, and I'll say them plainly now. The first is that **each animal contributes to one day only**: there are 49 animals, with 7, 8, 11, 12 and 11 of them on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30, because to look at the brain it has to be removed. Nobody was followed. The rows are independent, as they were in @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts for the NeuN counts, and what is missing is not a model for dependence between repeated measures but a model for the *shape* of the course. The second fact is one that the earlier chapters already mentioned, and that I would not want you to forget as the curves get prettier: **day 0 is the only sham group, and every later day is ischemic**. The step from day 0 to day 3 therefore mixes time with condition, and everything I say below about a "baseline" level at day 0 is a statement about sham-operated animals.

## A straight line, a polynomial, and why neither will do {#sec-lt-line-poly}

You have seen the straight line fail on this range already: in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions its residuals had group means of about -0.9, +2.3, +0.4, -2.1 and +0.8 mm² at the five days, which is a curve drawn in the residuals. I am going to fit it once more here, so that it is on the same footing as the models that come after it, and fit the next tool that most of us reach for when a line fails: a polynomial. A cubic is the usual second try, a line that is allowed to bend twice. Both are `brms` models with the priors written out. For the line, the intercept is the tissue area at day 0 (`Normal(14, 5)` mm², wide around the sham mean of the EDA chapters), the slope is a change in mm² per day (`Normal(0, 0.5)`, which allows 15 mm² in 30 days in either direction) and `sigma` is `Exponential(0.5)` as in the earlier chapters. For the cubic, the coefficients of the orthogonal polynomial are not interpretable one by one, so I only ask that they not be absurdly large (`Normal(0, 10)`).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Straight line over the whole 0 to 30 range (day 0 is the intercept)
fit_line <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data,
  prior = c(prior(normal(14, 5), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b), prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma)),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit1.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# Cubic polynomial of the day (orthogonal polynomial terms)
fit_cubic <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ poly(DPI, 3), data = cell_data,
  prior = c(prior(normal(12, 5), class = Intercept), prior(normal(0, 10), class = b), prior(exponential(0.5), class = sigma)),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit2.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::








I drew both curves out to day 45, deliberately beyond the last day we measured (@fig-lt_line_poly), because the question of what a model does where it has no data is the quickest way to tell a model with a mechanism from a model with a shape.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

  geom_vline(xintercept = 30, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30, 45)) +
  labs(x = "Days after the lesion (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme
```

@fig-lt_line_poly is the argument of this section. The straight line is wrong inside the data, which you know, and the interval narrowness is the dangerous part: the band is thin because the model is confident about a line, and the line is not the course. The cubic follows the five day means, because with five distinct days a polynomial has enough freedom to pass close to all of them. But look between day 14 and day 30, where nobody was measured: it dips to 4.3 mm² near day 23.5, below the smallest section in the whole file (5.9 mm²), and then comes back up to meet the day-30 mean. After day 30 it does what polynomials do outside the data: it turns, and its band widens to a range that has stopped meaning anything (at day 45 the median is 64.4 mm² with a 95% band from 39.9 to 88.2). McElreath and Gelman, Hill and Vehtari say the same thing in different words: a polynomial is a global shape, so a point at one end of the axis can change the curve arbitrarily far away from it, and it explodes outside the range of the data [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. Neither of them wants you to use high-order polynomials as a model of a time course, and the coefficients of a cubic have no biological meaning, so there is no number in the output that you could compare with another experiment.

Before I leave the line, the check that a fit should always pass: replicate the data from the model and look at the day means (@fig-lt_ppc_line). I use `bayesplot::ppc_stat_grouped()`, which draws, for each day, the distribution of the mean of replicated datasets and marks the observed mean, because a mean per day is exactly the feature that a line is bad at.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Replicated tissue areas from the line, summarized as the mean of each day
yrep_line <- posterior_predict(fit_line, ndraws = 500)

# Share of replicated means above the observed mean, by day (values near 0 or 1 mean the line cannot produce that mean)
ppp_line <- sapply(levels(cell_data$DPI_f), function(d) {
  idx <- cell_data$DPI_f == d
  mean(rowMeans(yrep_line[, idx, drop = FALSE]) >= mean(cell_data$Tissue_Area[idx]))
})
days_off <- names(ppp_line)[ppp_line < 0.05 | ppp_line > 0.95]
bayesplot::ppc_stat_grouped(y = cell_data$Tissue_Area, yrep = yrep_line, group = cell_data$DPI_f, stat = "mean", facet_args = list(nrow = 1)) +
  Plot_theme + legend_none() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Mean tissue area (mm²)")
```

If the line were an adequate description, the observed mean (the dark vertical line) would sit inside the replicated histogram in every panel. In @fig-lt_ppc_line it falls in the extreme 5% tail at day(s) 3, 14 (the share of replicated means above the observed one is 0.80, 0.00, 0.27, 1.00, 0.17 at days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30). This is the same message as the residuals of the assumptions chapter, now with the right amount of uncertainty drawn around it. I'll keep the line and the cubic in the comparison at the end of the chapter, because a comparison is only fair if the models you reject are in it.

## A curve with a meaning {#sec-lt-nonlinear}

What I want instead of a shape is a curve whose parameters I could say aloud in the lab. A **[nonlinear regression model]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** is one where the mean depends on the predictors through a formula that has parameters with a name and a meaning, instead of one coefficient per term. A thermostat is a good picture. A line says "the temperature changes 0.3 degrees per minute, forever". A thermostat says "the room is at 21 degrees now, it is cooling toward 15, and it loses half of the gap every ten minutes". The second sentence has three numbers that mean something, it cannot predict negative temperatures, and it says where the story is going. McElreath calls models like this scientific models and builds them from the process that generates the data [@mcelreath2020]; Gelman and colleagues make the same point about parameters you can check against physical reality [@gelman2026].

For the scar I need two ideas in one curve. One is **decay to a plateau**: tissue is lost over the weeks after the lesion and the loss levels off, which a thermostat sentence captures with an initial level, a plateau and a rate. The other is a **transient bump** around day 3, which the mean of day 3 shows (the area is *larger* than that of the sham animals) and which a decay alone cannot make. I read that bump as swelling of the tissue, edema, that precedes its loss, and I read the fall as atrophy. This is a hypothesis that the five days are compatible with, not something they prove: the curve describes the area of the section, and the data do not know why it is large.

<!-- TODO(Daniel): confirm the biological reading of the bump (edema) and of the fall (atrophy), and whether the day-3 spread in tissue area has a known technical cause. -->

Here is the formula. With $t$ the day after the lesion, the expected tissue area is

$$
\mu(t) \;=\; \underbrace{p + (a_0 - p)\,e^{-k t}}_{\text{decay to a plateau}} \;+\; \underbrace{h\, e^{-(t - t_p)^2 / (2 w^2)}}_{\text{transient bump}},
$$ {#eq-lt-bump}

and every parameter is a quantity I can read on the area axis or on the day axis: $a_0$ is the level at day 0 (the sham animals), $p$ the plateau toward which the area decays, $k$ the rate of decay per day (so $\ln 2 / k$ is the half-life of the gap), $h$ the extra area at the top of the bump, $t_p$ the day of the top and $w$ how wide it is in days (@tbl-lt_params).

### Priors for a curve are priors for the curve

The rule from @sec-priors-regularization is to judge a prior by the data it proposes. For a curve this means by the *curves* it proposes, not by the numbers it puts on its parameters, because a pair of parameters that each look reasonable can produce a curve that no animal could have. McElreath, the authors of the Bayesian workflow and Inchausti all make this the standard check for nonlinear models, and the way to run it in `brms` is to fit the model with `sample_prior = "only"` and draw the curves [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2026; @inchausti2023]. @tbl-lt_params has the prior of every parameter and the reason, stated in the units of the outcome, and @fig-lt_prior_curves shows the curves they imply.






::: {#tbl-lt_params .cell tbl-cap='Parameters of the curve for tissue area, what each one means and the prior I gave it with the reason.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One row per parameter of eq-lt-bump: meaning, prior and why that prior
params_tbl <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("a0", "plateau", "k", "h", "tp", "w", "sigma"),
  Meaning = c("Area at day 0 (sham animals), mm²", "Area toward which the tissue decays, mm²", "Rate of decay, per day",
              "Extra area at the top of the bump, mm²", "Day of the top of the bump", "Width of the bump, days", "Spread of the animals around the curve, mm²"),
  Prior = c("Normal(14, 4)", "Normal(8, 4), above 0", "LogNormal(log 0.08, 0.6)", "Normal(0, 3)", "Normal(3, 1.5), between 0.5 and 10", "LogNormal(log 2, 0.4)", "Exponential(0.5)"),
  Reason = c("Sections of 10 to 18 mm² are common in the sham mice of the earlier chapters", "Cannot be negative; the smallest section in the file is 5.9 mm², so the plateau is a few mm² below the sham level",
             "Half-lives of 3 to 30 days (k from 0.23 to 0.02) cover everything the biology allows; median 8.7 days", "Allows a bump of either sign of up to a few mm², about the day-3 scatter",
             "The bump is an early event; the first measurement after the lesion is day 3", "A bump a few days wide, not a month and not a day", "Mean 2 mm², as in the earlier chapters")
)
knitr::kable(params_tbl)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# The curve of eq-lt-bump, written for brms with nl = TRUE (each parameter gets its own formula and prior)
f_bump <- bf(Tissue_Area ~ plateau + (a0 - plateau) * exp(-k * DPI) + h * exp(-(DPI - tp)^2 / (2 * w^2)),
             a0 + plateau + k + h + tp + w ~ 1, nl = TRUE)

# The priors of the table above
pr_decay <- c(prior(normal(14, 4), nlpar = "a0"), prior(normal(8, 4), nlpar = "plateau", lb = 0),
              prior(lognormal(log(0.08), 0.6), nlpar = "k", lb = 0), prior(exponential(0.5), class = "sigma"))
pr_bump <- c(pr_decay, prior(normal(0, 3), nlpar = "h"), prior(normal(3, 1.5), nlpar = "tp", lb = 0.5, ub = 10),
             prior(lognormal(log(2), 0.4), nlpar = "w", lb = 0))

# Fit with priors only (no likelihood), to see the curves the priors propose
fit_bump_prior <- brm(f_bump, data = cell_data, prior = pr_bump, sample_prior = "only",
                      chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, refresh = 0,
                      file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit5.rds", file_refit = "never")
```
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Evaluate the curve of every prior draw on a grid of days, and keep 50 draws
curve_fun <- function(d, t) with(d, b_plateau_Intercept + (b_a0_Intercept - b_plateau_Intercept) * exp(-b_k_Intercept * t) +
                                    b_h_Intercept * exp(-(t - b_tp_Intercept)^2 / (2 * b_w_Intercept^2)))
grid30 <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.25)
dp <- as_draws_df(fit_bump_prior)
set.seed(1)
keep <- sample(nrow(dp), 50)
prior_curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(keep, function(i) data.frame(draw = i, DPI = grid30, mu = curve_fun(dp[i, ], grid30))))
share_prior_ok <- mean(prior_curves$mu > 0 & prior_curves$mu < 30)

# Thin lines for prior curves, the real animals on top
ggplot(prior_curves, aes(x = DPI, y = mu, group = draw)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days after the lesion (DPI)", y = "Tissue area (mm²)") +
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Each thin line is one curve that the priors consider possible before any animal is seen. Ask three things. Do the curves live in the part of the plane where tissue areas can live (here between 0 and about 30 mm²)? 100% of the curve values do. Do they differ from each other in the ways I am unsure about, bump or no bump, fast decay or slow? They do. And do the observed points look like a plausible draw from the cloud, not like an extreme value of it? They do. A good prior is not one that sits on top of the data; it is one that makes the data unsurprising without making them inevitable. The mistake to avoid is judging the prior by looking at each parameter's density on its own: it is the curve that has to make sense.
:::

Now the fit. Here is why I use `brms` for this model, and a thing I should be honest about. The model has six parameters for five distinct days, and most of what the data say is about the day means. A flat prior would leave several parameters poorly pinned, and the sampler would wander along a ridge in the likelihood where, for instance, a faster decay and a lower plateau give almost the same curve inside the observed days. The priors above are what pins the ridge down, and that is why I wrote them with care. The frequentist fit does not have that help, and I show what happens.


### Quantities you can ask of the curve {#sec-lt-derived}

The best reason to have a curve with a posterior is that the questions a reviewer asks are almost never about a parameter. They are about a day: *when was the area at its largest? When did it fall back to the level of the sham animals? How fast was it falling at day 14?* Each of these is a function of the curve, and any function of the parameters is itself a parameter with a full posterior: compute it row by row for each posterior draw and summarize the resulting vector [@mcelreath2020; @kruschke2015]. A [derived quantity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is the answer to a question you can say in the lab, computed from the parameters.

The half-eye is the figure to use when a quantity is a result and not a parameter, and @fig-lt_derived is the first of its kind in the chapter, so here is how to read it. The dot is the median, the thick bar the central 66% and the thin bar the central 95%, and the *shape* is part of the answer: a quantity that is a maximum or a crossing time, such as the day of the peak, often has a skewed or lumpy posterior, which is why I draw the whole distribution and not only a number with plus-or-minus. The book's authors warn about exactly this: the posterior of the location of a maximum or of a threshold crossing is often asymmetric, and a symmetric interval around a mean misleads [@mcelreath2020; @kruschke2015]. Here the day of the peak is 3.8 [2.6, 4.6] and the day on which the area is back at the day-0 level is 6.4 [4.3, 7.3], with an interval that is wide relative to the spacing of the measurements (the nearest days measured are 3 and 7), which is fair: the curve is an interpolation between them, and the interval is the model saying so. The rate at day 14, -0.18 [-0.27, -0.10] mm² per day, is the number that most resembles what the straight line of @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous called the slope, and the comparison is the point. That chapter's slope was -0.67 mm² per day, one rate for the whole window of days 3 to 14, which includes the steepest part of the fall. The curve says that the rate is not constant: by day 14 the area is still falling, but much more slowly. A line cannot say that, and a curve gives you the rate on the day you ask for.

A word on reading the curve outside what was measured. Between days 3 and 7 and between days 14 and 30 the curve is an interpolation, and the value at day 20 is the model's inference, not an observation. Past day 30 it is an extrapolation, and the model's answer is the plateau, a parameter with a weak data basis (above). I do not draw anything beyond day 30 for this model, and the next section shows what a model with no mechanism does there.

## Counting cells along the same course {#sec-lt-counts}

The same ideas apply to a count. The PDGFR-β+ cells of @sec-count-regression are a count of cells in a section whose area changes over the time course, so the model is the one of that chapter, a negative binomial with the area as an exposure, and the curve is not of the count but of the *density* (cells per mm²). The shape the data show (@fig-lt_hook, middle panel) is a rise that begins after day 3 and a decline by day 30. A curve that can rise from a low level, peak and come down is a **pulse**: $d(t) = b + A\,[(t/t_{pk})\,e^{1 - t/t_{pk}}]^{s}$, where $b$ is the density before the rise (cells per mm²), $A$ the extra density at the top of the pulse, $t_{pk}$ the day of the top and $s$ how sharply it rises (the larger, the later and steeper). It has the same virtue as the one above: every parameter is on a scale I can say aloud. I use priors that follow the counts of @sec-count-regression: a baseline density of about 30 cells per mm² (`Normal(30, 15)`), an amplitude of a few hundred (`Normal(300, 150)`), a peak between days 3 and 30 (`Normal(14, 5)`), and the default prior of that chapter for the dispersion `shape`.

## A curve without a recipe: the Gaussian process {#sec-lt-gp}

Suppose that I do not trust my own recipe. The decay and the bump are a story I told about the area, and the five days would be equally happy with a different story. What I want then is a curve that is allowed to be anything *smooth*, and that tells me how smooth it thinks it is. That is what a **[Gaussian process]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** (GP) gives you. The picture to hold is a group of friends standing along a rope, one at every day: friends who stand close are likely to be at similar heights, and friends who stand far apart are not. A GP is a prior over whole curves built from that one idea, that the height at one day is correlated with the height at a nearby day, and the correlation fades with the distance between them. It has two knobs, and each one has a picture.

- The **[length-scale]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** ($\ell$) is how far you have to move along the rope before the height has "forgotten" where it was: how many days apart two friends must stand before they stop resembling each other. A long length-scale gives slow, gentle curves; a short one gives a curve that wiggles from day to day.
- The **[marginal standard deviation]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}** (the amplitude, $\alpha$) is how high the curve can wander from its average: how tall the tallest oscillation can be.

@fig-lt_gp_draws shows both knobs at work before any data enter. Each panel has five curves drawn from a GP prior; length-scales grow from the left to the right panel and the amplitude from the top row to the bottom one.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Draw curves from a zero-mean GP with a squared-exponential covariance, on a grid of days
gp_draws <- function(ell, alpha, grid, n = 5, seed = 11) {
  set.seed(seed)
  K <- alpha^2 * exp(-outer(grid, grid, "-")^2 / (2 * ell^2)) + diag(1e-8, length(grid))
  z <- matrix(rnorm(length(grid) * n), length(grid), n)
  as.vector(t(chol(K)) %*% z)
}
grid_gp <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.5)
gp_demo <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(2, 8, 30), function(ell) do.call(rbind, lapply(c(2, 4), function(a) {
  data.frame(DPI = rep(grid_gp, 5), draw = rep(1:5, each = length(grid_gp)), value = gp_draws(ell, a, grid_gp),
             ell = paste("length-scale", ell, "days"), amp = paste("amplitude", a, "mm²"))
}))))
gp_demo$ell <- factor(gp_demo$ell, levels = paste("length-scale", c(2, 8, 30), "days"))

# One panel per pair of knobs
ggplot(gp_demo, aes(x = DPI, y = value, group = draw, color = factor(draw))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(amp ~ ell) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#000000", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "Deviation from the average curve (mm²)") +
  Plot_theme + legend_none()
```

Each line is one curve that the prior considers possible, and the question is what the knobs do to the *family* of curves. Read across a row: as the length-scale grows, curves lose their fast wiggles and become gentler, until at 30 days they barely bend within the observed range. Read down a column: a larger amplitude spreads the curves vertically but leaves their wiggliness unchanged. A good prior lets the data pick among these families, and does not forbid the ones that the data support. The mistake to avoid is to think of the GP as having no assumptions: its assumption is smoothness, and the length-scale is how much.
:::

Two things about the data make the length-scale a delicate choice here. The days we measured are 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30, so the closest two are 3 days apart. A GP is free to propose a length-scale of a day or less, a curve that wiggles between two measured days, and the five days cannot contradict it, because no animal was measured in between. The books that explain GPs, McElreath and the authors of the Bayesian workflow, recommend a prior that puts almost no mass on length-scales smaller than the distance between the nearest measurements, and a family that does this is the inverse-gamma [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2026]. I use `InvGamma(3, 15)`, which has its mass between about 3 and 50 days (median 5.6 days), and an `Exponential(0.5)` for the amplitude (mean 2 mm²). `brms` writes this model with `gp(DPI)`; I set `scale = FALSE` so that the length-scale is in days and not in a rescaled unit.

Read @fig-lt_gp_vs_mech as an argument about what each model is for, and look at two things in it. At the days that were measured, the two curves are almost the same line, and that is the reassuring result: the story I told (decay plus bump) is not forcing the answer, because a model with no story draws nearly the same medians. Between and beyond those days they part company, and the bands are the lesson. The GP is honest about not having measured anything between day 14 and day 30: its band opens to a range of about 3 to 15 mm² there, and drifts back to its average after day 30. The mechanistic band stays narrow in the same gaps. It is narrow *because of its formula*, which insists on a smooth fall to a plateau, and not because the animals said so; if the formula is right the narrow band is a gain, and if it is wrong it is overconfidence. That is the right division of labor: use the curve with a meaning when you have a theory and you want interpretable parameters and a defensible statement about where the process is going; use the GP when you want to *describe* the shape without committing to a formula, and stay within the days you measured. I do not teach splines here, which are the other way of letting a curve bend, and have a chapter of their own (@sec-causal-inference-splines); a GP and a spline are close relatives, and the `mgcv` smooth above is one of them.

### Which curve predicts better? {#sec-lt-loo}

I have now six ways of describing the same five days: the line, the cubic, the decay, the decay with the bump, the Gaussian process and, as the reference, one free mean for every day (the model of @sec-linear-models-reflection, with a single spread). Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) ranks them by how well each predicts an animal that it did not see [@vehtari2017]. I include the line and the cubic on purpose: a comparison is only informative if the models that you reject are in it, and a model that wins against a straw man has told you nothing. I report the difference of each model from the best one *in units of its standard error*, because a difference of 9 elpd points with a standard error of 9 is not a difference.






::: {#tbl-lt_loo .cell tbl-cap='Leave-one-out comparison of the models for tissue area. elpd_diff is the difference in expected log predictive density from the best model (0 is the best, more negative is worse); se_diff its standard error; Pareto k counts observations with k above 0.7 after moment matching.'}

First, the straight line and the simple decay (with no bump) are clearly behind the others (about 3.5 standard errors behind the best model, -21 and -18 elpd points): the bump matters, and the line is the worst model. I know of no such process here. A covariate that explains the split is the first thing to look for, and I have looked at the ones the file has; none of them separates the groups. What remains is to say what the data allow. **At day 30 the animals divide into two groups by the extent of GFAP-positive tissue, I do not know why, and eleven animals cannot tell a mixture of two populations from a wide single one.** I therefore do not fit a mixture. ## From a curve across animals to animals across time {#sec-lt-repeated}

Everything so far has treated time as a comparison between different animals, and I said that this was one half of the story. The other half starts with a different experiment. In the open-field test, which we met in @sec-beta-robust-regression, a mouse is placed in an arena for five minutes and the tracker records where it goes. The same mice were tested before the lesion (day 0, the baseline) and on days 1, 4, 8, 15 and 22 after it. That is a **[longitudinal design]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}**: the same animals followed through time, so that each animal's days belong together. Two things follow, and they are the two new ideas of the rest of the chapter. A mouse that spent a lot of time in the center on one day will tend to do the same on the next (the observations of one animal are not independent, the problem that [the introduction to this part](multilevel-intro.qmd#sec-multilevel-intro) put at the center), and the days are not evenly spaced: the first two are a day apart, the last two a week.

![A path across uneven stepping stones. The same walker crosses at the same speed, but the stones are one, three, four, seven and seven paces apart: how far two stones are from each other is part of how much they resemble each other.](images/longitudinal-timeseries_uneven-stepping-stones.png){#fig-lt-stones fig-align="center" width="80%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a small white mouse standing on the third of six flat stones crossing a stream. The first two stones almost touch and the gaps grow wider toward the right, with dashed arcs marking the jumps between stones."}

Think of the second idea as a mouse crossing a stream on uneven stepping stones: the spacing matters, because a day-1 session is likely to look more like day 0 than a day-22 session looks like day 15, simply because it is closer in time. @fig-lt-stones draws the stones.


### The file, with the rules of the earlier chapter {#sec-lt-of-data}

The data are the open-field table of @sec-beta-robust-regression, and I do not reopen any of its decisions. The animal is identified by the `Animal` column (with the leading `M` and zeros stripped, because the same mouse is written `M011` on day 0 and `11` on later days); the animals whose treatment label changes between days are left out altogether; a session needs at least 270 of its 300 seconds tracked; and the zeros stay in. There, the analysis used day 1 only. Here every day is used. The chunk is the preparation of that chapter, written for all days, and the `stopifnot()` is the check that I get its counts.

```{.r .cell-code}

of_raw <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/OpenField_Summary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)

# One row per animal and test day; times in seconds. The animal is identified by Animal, not by ReCode
of <- data.frame(
  animal = sub("^0+", "", sub("^M", "", of_raw$Animal)),
  label = of_raw$Treatment,
  dpi = of_raw$DPI,
  distance = of_raw$Distance,
  mean_speed = of_raw$Mean_Speed,
  center = of_raw[["Center : time"]],
  arena = of_raw[["Arena : time"]],
  borders = of_raw[["Borders : time"]]
)
of$tracked <- of$center + of$arena + of$borders

# Animals whose treatment label changes between days are excluded, as in the earlier chapter
labels_per <- tapply(of$label, of$animal, function(z) length(unique(z)))
bad_animals <- names(which(labels_per > 1))
n_raw_strings <- length(unique(of_raw$Animal))
n_animals <- length(unique(of$animal))

# The four groups of the earlier chapter, all days, sessions with at least 270 s tracked
groups4 <- c("WildType", "WT-Sham", "Klf4-KO", "KO-Sham")
make_of <- function(min_tracked = 270) {
  keep <- !(of$animal %in% bad_animals) & of$label %in% groups4 & of$tracked > 0 & of$tracked >= min_tracked
  z <- of[keep, ]
  z$genotype <- factor(ifelse(grepl("KO", z$label), "KO", "WT"), levels = c("WT", "KO"))
  z$surgery <- factor(ifelse(grepl("Sham", z$label), "sham", "ischemia"), levels = c("sham", "ischemia"))
  z$group <- factor(paste(z$genotype, z$surgery), levels = c("WT sham", "WT ischemia", "KO sham", "KO ischemia"))
  z$share <- z$center / z$tracked
  z <- z[order(z$animal, z$dpi), ]
  z$an <- factor(z$animal)
  z$dpi_f <- factor(z$dpi)
  z$isch <- as.numeric(z$surgery == "ischemia")
  z$ko <- as.numeric(z$genotype == "KO")
  z$post <- as.numeric(z$dpi > 0)
  # Time on a log scale, centered (used for a varying slope over time)
  z$lt <- log1p(z$dpi) - mean(log1p(c(0, 1, 4, 8, 15, 22)))
  z
}
ofl <- make_of()

# Counts of the earlier chapter: 79 raw strings, 69 animals, 7 labels that change; 38 animals on day 1
stopifnot(n_raw_strings == 79, n_animals == 69, length(bad_animals) == 7, sum(ofl$dpi == 1) == 38)

n_sessions <- nrow(ofl)
days_per_animal <- table(table(ofl$animal))
```

## Building the model, one rung at a time {#sec-lt-ladder}

A good model of repeated measures is not written down in one go; it is built from the picture, one feature at a time, and each step has to answer something that you can see in @fig-lt_spaghetti. The same strategy as in @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes, and I will keep the outcome of @sec-beta-robust-regression: a zero-inflated beta for the share of the tracked time, with its precision `phi` (the later `brms` default for the family, with the scale of the earlier chapter) and a probability of a structural zero `zi` that is a single number, since the zeros are few (8 of 246 sessions). There are four rungs.

1. **Rung 0, the rows as independent.** One mean for each group and day, as if each session came from a different animal. This is the model the earlier chapter used at day 1, extended to all days, and it is the baseline of the comparison.
2. **Rung 1, a varying intercept for the animal** (`(1 | animal)`). A line of the figure that starts high tends to stay high: the animal has a level of its own. This is @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts.
3. **Rung 2, a varying intercept and a varying slope over time, correlated** (`(1 + time | animal)`). Some animals change more than others, and the model should say how much (@sec-multilevel-varying-slopes). The slope is over the logarithm of one plus the day (`log1p`, centered), because the same number of days matters more early than late: the stepping stones are not evenly spaced and the changes are fast at the beginning.
4. **Rung 3, a curve in time by group.** The means of 24 cells (4 groups, 6 days) are many numbers for a pattern with a simple description: in the sham groups, nothing; in the ischemic ones a jump at day 1 and a decay back to the baseline. This is the nonlinear idea of the first half of the chapter, now on the logit scale, with one jump per genotype: @eq-lt-spike.

$$
\text{logit}(\mu_{ij}) \;=\; b_0 + u_i + \underbrace{I_i\, P_j\, A_{g[i]}\, e^{-(t_j - 1)/\tau}}_{\text{spike and return, ischemic animals after the lesion}}, \qquad u_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_u),
$$ {#eq-lt-spike}

with $I_i$ equal to 1 for an animal that had an ischemia, $P_j$ equal to 1 after the lesion (day 1 onwards), $A_g$ the size of the jump of genotype $g$ on the logit scale, $\tau$ the number of days in which the excess falls by a factor $e$ (so $\tau \ln 2$ is its half-life) and $u_i$ the level of animal $i$. The sham animals follow only $b_0 + u_i$. I give $b_0$ a `Normal(-3, 1.5)` (a baseline share of about 5%, between 1% and 20%), each $A_g$ a `Normal(1.5, 1)` (a jump that can multiply the odds of being in the center by a factor between 1 and 30), $\tau$ a `LogNormal(log 3, 0.6)` (half-lives between about 1 and 9 days) and $\sigma_u$ an `Exponential(2)`, and `phi` and the zero part get the priors of the earlier chapter.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Common priors: baseline and effects on the logit scale, spread of animals, precision and zero part
pr_fix <- c(prior(normal(-3, 1.5), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"))
pr_phi <- prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = "phi")
pr_zi <- prior(normal(-2, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi")
pr_sd <- prior(exponential(2), class = "sd")

# Rung 0: one mean per group and day, rows treated as independent
fit_r0 <- brm(bf(share ~ group * dpi_f, zi ~ 1), data = ofl, family = zero_inflated_beta(),
              prior = c(pr_fix, pr_phi, pr_zi), chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit20.rds", file_refit = "never")

# Rung 1: the same means, plus a level for each animal
fit_r1 <- brm(bf(share ~ group * dpi_f + (1 | an), zi ~ 1), data = ofl, family = zero_inflated_beta(),
              prior = c(pr_fix, pr_phi, pr_zi, pr_sd), chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit21.rds", file_refit = "never")

# Rung 2: a level and a slope over (log) time for each animal, correlated (LKJ prior as in the previous chapter)
fit_r2 <- brm(bf(share ~ group * dpi_f + (1 + lt | an), zi ~ 1), data = ofl, family = zero_inflated_beta(),
              prior = c(pr_fix, pr_phi, pr_zi, pr_sd, prior(lkj(2), class = "cor")), chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit22.rds", file_refit = "never")

# Rung 3: spike and return, written for brms with nl = TRUE; the link (logit) is applied by brms to the whole expression
f_spike <- bf(share ~ b0 + u + post * isch * (aw * (1 - ko) + ak * ko) * exp(-(dpi - 1) / tau),
              b0 + aw + ak + tau ~ 1, u ~ 0 + (1 | an), zi ~ 1, nl = TRUE)
pr_spike <- c(prior(normal(-3, 1.5), nlpar = "b0"), prior(normal(1.5, 1), nlpar = "aw"), prior(normal(1.5, 1), nlpar = "ak"),
              prior(lognormal(log(3), 0.6), nlpar = "tau", lb = 0), prior(exponential(2), class = "sd", nlpar = "u"), pr_phi, pr_zi)
fit_r3 <- brm(f_spike, data = ofl, family = zero_inflated_beta(), prior = pr_spike,
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit23.rds", file_refit = "never")
```

@tbl-lt_ladder is the ladder in one table.













Read it from the top. The best rung is the spike and return with a level for each animal (rung 3), and it is also the one with the fewest parameters: the 24 free means of the other rungs are replaced by four numbers that mean something. Rung 1, with the same animal level but 24 free means, is 10 elpd points behind (3.2 standard errors), and rung 0, which treats the 246 sessions as independent, is 25 behind with a standard error of 18: a large gap measured imprecisely, which is what you would expect from a model that counts the sessions of one animal as separate pieces of evidence. What the level of the animal is worth can be read in its spread, 0.64 [0.49, 0.84] on the logit scale: an animal one standard deviation above the average has about 1.9 times the odds of being in the center of an animal at the average.

Rung 2 deserves a sentence of its own, because it is the one that continues @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes and it does not pay. The varying slope over time ranks the same as rung 1 (about 1 elpd point apart, well within one standard error), its spread is 0.17 [0.02, 0.33] and its correlation with the level is -0.53 [-0.92, 0.27], an interval that runs from strongly negative to positive, and 8 sessions have a Pareto k above 0.7 even after moment matching. The picture asked for the slope and the data do not support it: with six sessions of which most lie on the flat part of the course, a slope for each animal is not something the data can estimate. The books warn that slopes and a residual dependence structure compete for the same information in small samples [@inchausti2023; @gelman2020], and the next section will show the same thing with another pair of terms. The varying intercept is the part of the structure that the data hold up.

**Frequentist equivalent.** `glmmTMB` agrees on the first two rungs: the level for each animal improves the AIC from -819 to -860, and its standard deviation is 0.63 on the logit scale, close to the Bayesian one. It disagrees where it matters for rung 2. The fit with a varying slope returns a correlation of exactly -1 between the level and the slope and a Hessian that is not positive definite, so it has no AIC to report (NA): this is the singular fit of @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes, in which the data cannot distinguish the correlation from the boundary of its range. The Bayesian fit of the same model returns a finite correlation with an honest interval, because the LKJ prior keeps it off the boundary, and it is the more useful of the two for saying that the slope is not supported. The nonlinear rung 3 has no counterpart in `glmmTMB` for a beta outcome, which is why it is only in the left tab.

### Does the model reproduce the data? {#sec-lt-ppc}

A model can rank first in a comparison and still be wrong about the thing that you care about, so before going on I ask rung 3 to generate fake datasets and I look at two features of the real one that the beta is likely to miss: how large the largest share is and how spread the shares are. They are the features that a single precision `phi` for all sessions constrains, because a beta with a fixed precision has only so much room around its mean. @fig-lt_ppc_rungs shows the answer for rung 3 and for the same model with one more term, a level for each *session* (an [observation-level random effect]{.ix ix="observation-level random effect"}, the device of @sec-multilevel-glmm for variation that a family does not carry).

## Do neighboring days resemble each other more than distant ones? {#sec-lt-dependence}

The fourth feature on the list was the dependence between days, and it is the one that the word "time series" brings to mind. Imagine a mouse whose day-4 session was unusually timid. The question is whether the next session is also timid *because it is the next one*, so that the resemblance decays as the sessions move apart, or because the mouse is a timid animal, so that the resemblance is the same whatever the gap. The two models differ. In a model with a [varying intercept]{.ix ix="varying intercept"} (rung 1) every pair of sessions of an animal has the same correlation, whatever the gap; this is called [compound symmetry]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, and it is the structure that a single random effect implies. In an [autoregressive model of order one]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (AR(1)) each session carries over a fraction $\rho$ of the previous one's deviation, so that the correlation between sessions $k$ steps apart is $\rho^k$, decaying with the gap. The two can be told apart by looking, before any model, at how the correlation between the leftovers of two days depends on how far apart the days are.

For this look I do not need the beta family. The leftover of a session is the distance from its group-and-day mean, and the logit of the share (for the sessions with a positive share) is a scale where those distances are comparable across days. For every pair of days I compute the correlation of the leftovers across the animals that have both, and plot it against the gap in days (@fig-lt_resid_lag), which is the empirical cousin of what a variogram shows for spatial data.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Leftovers of the logit of the share from the group-by-day means (positive shares only)
ofp <- ofl[ofl$share > 0, ]
ofp$lg <- qlogis(ofp$share)
ofp$res <- resid(lm(lg ~ group * dpi_f, data = ofp))

# One row per animal, one column per day
res_w <- reshape(ofp[, c("animal", "dpi", "res")], idvar = "animal", timevar = "dpi", direction = "wide")
days <- c(0, 1, 4, 8, 15, 22)
pairs_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(combn(seq_along(days), 2, simplify = FALSE), function(ix) {
  a <- res_w[[paste0("res.", days[ix[1]])]]; b <- res_w[[paste0("res.", days[ix[2]])]]
  ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
  data.frame(d1 = days[ix[1]], d2 = days[ix[2]], gap = days[ix[2]] - days[ix[1]], r = cor(a[ok], b[ok]), n = sum(ok),
             early = days[ix[1]] %in% c(0, 1))
}))
pairs_df$kind <- ifelse(pairs_df$early, "involves day 0 or day 1", "days 4 to 22")
cor_later <- pairs_df[!pairs_df$early, ]
```

Each point answers one question: do the leftovers of day A and day B go together across the animals? A value near 0 says no, a value of 0.5 says that animals above their group's mean on one day tend to be above it on the other. The shape of the points against the gap is the diagnosis. If dependence were serial, the points would fall as the gap grows (high at 1 or 3 days, close to zero at 14 or 21). If it were compound symmetry, they would sit at the same height for every gap. The mistake to avoid is to read a single point: each rests on 24 to 47 animals, and a correlation from 30 pairs has an interval of about plus or minus 0.3.

The blue points of @fig-lt_resid_lag are flat: the correlation among days 4, 8, 15 and 22 is between 0.25 and 0.53, and it does not fall as the gap grows from 4 to 18 days (the slope of the line is -0.002 per day). The orange points are lower and scattered: the baseline and the first day correlate weakly with the rest, -0.08 to 0.55. This is a result that I did not expect when I started, because I had in mind the serial flavor of dependence that the assumptions chapter describes, and it is better to say so than to bend the analysis to the expectation. In these mice, once the lesion has had its first day, a mouse tends to stay the mouse that it is: *an animal-level trait*, not a memory of the previous session. The first two sessions are different because they are the baseline and the day of the spike, whose size is not predicted by the animal's usual behavior.

To put numbers on it and to compare structures I use the Gaussian model on the logit scale of the same sessions with a positive share (238 of 246), the family that `brms` supports for autocorrelation terms. I should say what I tried first. The `ar()` term of `brms` did not run with the beta family (the sampler could not be initialized), and the sessions without a positive share cannot be put on the logit scale, so the comparison below is a *sensitivity analysis* with a different likelihood, not a refit of the rungs. There are four models, all with group-by-day means: a varying intercept for the animal; an AR(1) residual correlation alone; both together; and compound symmetry (`cosy()`), which in `brms` is the residual version of a varying intercept.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors for the Gaussian models on the logit scale
pr_g <- c(prior(normal(-3, 2), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"), prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma"))

# Varying intercept for the animal
fit_d1 <- brm(lg ~ group * dpi_f + (1 | an), data = ofp, prior = c(pr_g, pr_sd),
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit24.rds", file_refit = "never")

# AR(1) residual correlation between consecutive sessions of an animal (time = day; the sessions are taken in order)
fit_d2 <- brm(bf(lg ~ group * dpi_f + ar(time = dpi, gr = an, p = 1)), data = ofp, prior = pr_g,
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit25.rds", file_refit = "never")

# Both: a level for each animal and AR(1) on top
fit_d3 <- brm(bf(lg ~ group * dpi_f + (1 | an) + ar(time = dpi, gr = an, p = 1)), data = ofp, prior = c(pr_g, pr_sd),
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit26.rds", file_refit = "never")

# Compound symmetry: the same correlation between every pair of sessions of an animal
fit_d4 <- brm(bf(lg ~ group * dpi_f + cosy(time = dpi, gr = an)), data = ofp, prior = pr_g,
              chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, save_pars = sp, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit27.rds", file_refit = "never")
```
:::






A word on what the `ar()` term of `brms` does with unequally spaced sessions, because it is the reason for a warning that I have to give. It orders the sessions of an animal by `time` and treats consecutive sessions as one step apart, whatever the days between them. For sessions at days 0, 1, 4, 8, 15 and 22 this makes the step from day 15 to day 22 as strong a link as the step from day 0 to day 1, which is not what serial dependence in time would do [@inchausti2023; @harrell2015]. The correct tool for unequal spacing is a **continuous-time** correlation, in which the correlation between two sessions is $\rho^{|t_1 - t_2|}$ with the gap in days in the exponent (the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which is the continuous-time version of an AR(1)). It is available in the frequentist tools, `nlme::corCAR1` and `glmmTMB::ou()`, and `brms` has none of its own; so the frequentist tab is not an afterthought here but the way to do what the Bayesian tab cannot.

@tbl-lt_dep gives the verdict of the comparison, and it agrees with the figure. A level for each animal and compound symmetry are the same model in two spellings and rank the same (-0.2 elpd points apart). Adding an AR(1) term to the level does not help (-6.2 points, standard error 3.5), and AR(1) *instead of* the level is behind (-9.2). The estimates say the same in numbers: the correlation of compound symmetry is 0.31 [0.17, 0.47]; the AR coefficient alone is 0.35 [0.21, 0.49], but once a level for the animal is in the model it falls to 0.23 [-0.02, 0.45], an interval that includes zero, while the spread of the animal levels goes from 0.57 to 0.36. The two terms are competing for the same dependence, which is the identifiability problem that the literature on repeated measures warns about [@inchausti2023], and the data cannot say how to divide it between them. The compact reading is that the animal-level correlation is the structure that the data support, and that a serial term on top of it is not needed to describe them.

**Frequentist equivalent.** The continuous-time tools, which are the correct ones for these unequal gaps, tell the same story, and one of them tells it in a disguised way that is worth knowing about. With `nlme`, a level for the animal has an AIC of 701.8; adding a continuous-time AR(1) term (`corCAR1`) does not improve it (703.8), and the continuous-time term alone is 21 AIC points worse. The best that `corCAR1` can do alone is a correlation of 0.14 for sessions one day apart, which has vanished a week later; that is a poor description of the flat 0.3 to 0.5 of @fig-lt_resid_lag, and it is why the level wins. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck term of `glmmTMB` for the beta outcome looks, at first, like a triumph: its AIC is 123 points better than the level. But look at what it estimated: a correlation of 0.12 between sessions one day apart and none beyond, together with a beta precision that runs off to about 7,000. It has stopped describing a memory in time and has become a variance for each single session. Putting the level back in with the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck term, the correlation parameter goes to zero, and the result has the same AIC as a level plus a variance for each session (-1005 against -1007). In plain words, the gain was not serial dependence; it was the extra variation between sessions that the beta cannot carry on its own, which is exactly what the predictive check of the previous section found. I would not use either term to claim a decay in time.

What these mice say about the question of this section is therefore short. Within an animal, the sessions after day 1 resemble each other as the trait of one mouse, and the data do not show a serial memory on top of it; a short-range serial dependence between neighboring days is not excluded, but six unequally spaced sessions, with a spike on the second one, cannot estimate it. The independence discussion of the earlier chapters named two flavors of dependence, the one that is a trait of the animal and the one that is a memory of the previous session, and in these data the first is the one that is there.



## What to do with day 0: the baseline {#sec-lt-baseline}

Day 0 of the open field is a session before the lesion, and every animal has one (when its session was tracked). It is tempting to use it, and there are three standard ways. Before I describe them, notice what separates them from the first half of the chapter. In the histology data day 0 was a different group of animals (the sham ones), so it was a comparison group and not a baseline. Here day 0 is the *same animal* before the lesion, a baseline in the proper sense, and the question of how to use it becomes real.

The three ways differ in what they estimate. I use one concrete question, small enough to compute three times: **did the wild-type mice with an ischemia differ from the sham-operated ones on day 1, after taking their own day 0 into account?** The outcome is the logit of the share of time in the center, so that the answer is a difference in log odds (and its exponential a ratio of odds), and I keep the wild-type animals that have a positive share on both days.

1. **Change from baseline** (a "change score"): subtract each animal's day 0 from its day 1 and compare the changes between the two groups. It estimates the difference between the groups in the *average change*.
2. **Baseline as a covariate**: model the day-1 value with the group *and* the day-0 value as predictors, which asks how the groups differ on day 1 among animals with the same baseline. Harrell and Gelman, Hill and Vehtari agree on the reason for preferring it to the change score: the change score is the same model with the coefficient of the baseline forced to be exactly 1, and, because of measurement error and regression to the mean, the coefficient that the data support is usually less than 1 [@harrell2015; @gelman2020]. Letting the data choose gives a more precise estimate and does not pay for an assumption that the data may not honor.
3. **All days, with day 0 as one more time point**: a model for the whole trajectory with a level for each animal, in which the baseline enters as the first observation of the same animals. It uses every session, and it is the one that scales to six days.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Wild-type animals with a positive share on both day 0 and day 1; one row per animal in the wide table
wb <- ofl[ofl$genotype == "WT" & ofl$dpi %in% c(0, 1) & ofl$share > 0, ]
wb <- wb[wb$an %in% names(which(table(wb$an) == 2)), ]
wb$lg <- qlogis(wb$share)
wide <- reshape(wb[, c("an", "dpi", "lg", "isch")], idvar = c("an", "isch"), timevar = "dpi", direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- c("an", "isch", "base", "post")
wide$change <- wide$post - wide$base

# Priors for the three small models (log-odds scale)
pr_b <- c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"), prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma"))

# 1. Change score
fit_chg <- brm(change ~ isch, data = wide, prior = pr_b, chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
               file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit28.rds", file_refit = "never")
# 2. Baseline as a covariate
fit_cov <- brm(post ~ isch + base, data = wide, prior = pr_b, chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
               file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit29.rds", file_refit = "never")
# 3. Both days in one model, with a level for each animal (the ischemic group differs only after the lesion)
fit_all <- brm(lg ~ post + post:isch + (1 | an), data = wb, prior = c(pr_b, pr_sd), chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123, control = ctl, refresh = 0,
               file = "models/longitudinal-timeseries_fit30.rds", file_refit = "never")
```

I do not know from the file how the animals were assigned, and the validity of the second and third approaches depends on it, so I say it.

**What I recommend for these data.** For the course over the six days, the model with all days and day 0 as the first time point (the ladder of the previous section), because it uses every session, it is the only one of the three that generalizes beyond a single day, and the baseline enters as one observation of the same animal. For a question about one day only, the baseline as a covariate, because it lets the data weight the baseline. I would not use the change score: with a baseline that predicts this little of the later values, it only adds noise, and it does not protect against regression to the mean, which the covariate model handles [@harrell2015; @gelman2020]. None of this applies to the histology data of the first half of the chapter. There, day 0 is a group of different animals, the baseline is a comparison group and not a measurement of the same animal, and the right analysis is a model of the whole course that includes that group (as in @sec-lt-nonlinear); a change score is not even defined.

If a mouse that moves a lot, or that sits in a corner, is more likely to be lost by the tracker, the missing sessions are not a random sample of the sessions. The honest statement is the one of @sec-eda-missing-data: the data cannot tell whether they are missing at random, because the missing values are the only evidence.

What can be said is what each model assumes. Deleting every animal that lacks a session (complete cases) is not safe, and in this file it would leave only 25 of 48 animals. If the tracker loses a mouse because of what the mouse was doing, the missingness depends on the unobserved value, and no analysis of the observed data can repair that without an additional model of the loss; that is the territory of @sec-missing-data-measurement-error, and I do not enter it here. ## How to report it {#sec-lt-report}

Two blocks, one for each half of the chapter, written the way I would write them in a paper.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it: the course of the tissue area"}
**Results.** Tissue area was 14.8 [13.7, 16.0] mm² at day 0 (sham animals, n = 7), reached its largest value of 16.9 [15.7, 19.0] mm² at day 3.8 [2.6, 4.6] and was back at the day-0 level by day 6.4 [4.3, 7.3]. It then fell steadily: 9.6 [8.8, 10.4] mm² at day 14 (n = 12), falling at 0.18 [0.10, 0.27] mm² per day on that day, and 8.0 [7.1, 8.9] mm² at day 30 (n = 11), 8.9 [7.5, 11.2] mm² below the largest value (posterior medians and 95% credible intervals). The spread between animals was largest at day 3 (3.0 [2.0, 5.1] mm², against about 1.1 mm² at the other days). The curve is a statement about different animals at each day, and day 0 is a sham group.

**Methods.** The area of the section was modeled as a function of the day after the lesion with a decay to a plateau plus a Gaussian-shaped transient bump (six parameters; Normal(14, 4), Normal(8, 4), LogNormal(log 0.08, 0.6), Normal(0, 3), Normal(3, 1.5) and LogNormal(log 2, 0.4) priors for the level at day 0, the plateau, the rate, the height, the day and the width of the bump) with a Gaussian likelihood, in `brms` (four chains of 2,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). Each animal contributed to one day. A Gaussian process over the day gave the same curve at the measured days, and the plateau was not identified by the data (7.1 [3.8, 8.6] mm²) and is not reported as a result.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it: the open field over six days"}
**Results.** In the open field, the odds of being in the center on day 1 rose by a factor of 8.3 [5.2, 13.1] in wild-type mice and 6.2 [4.0, 9.8] in Klf4-KO mice with an ischemia, relative to their own baseline, and the excess decayed with a time constant of 2.5 [1.5, 3.7] days. The ratio of the two jumps (wild-type over Klf4-KO) was 1.3 [0.7, 2.5], with a posterior probability of 0.82 that it exceeds 1. Sham-operated animals showed no change over the six days. The correlation between two sessions of the same animal was about 0.31 [0.17, 0.47] after day 0, independent of the gap between them (238 sessions, 48 mice).

**Methods.** The share of the tracked time spent in the center (sessions with at least 270 s tracked) was modeled with a zero-inflated beta likelihood, with the logit of its mean following a baseline level, a level for each animal and for each session (`Exponential(2)` priors on their spreads; the session-level term was added because the model without it could not reproduce the largest shares) and a decaying excess on the days after the lesion in ischemic animals (@eq-lt-spike), in `brms` (four chains of 2,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400). Dependence between sessions was examined with the correlations of the residuals by gap and with Gaussian models on the logit scale that compared a level for each animal with an AR(1) structure. The animals with an inconsistent treatment label were excluded as in the earlier analysis of day 1.
:::

There is a curve for the scar and a model for the animals followed in time, and two things in this chapter are left open on purpose. One is the values that are missing for reasons that depend on what is missing: the sessions that the tracker lost, the section that could not be counted, the values below what a microscope can see. That is the subject of @sec-missing-data-measurement-error. The other is the curve itself: a spline is the third way to let a line bend, next to the mechanistic curve and the Gaussian process of this chapter, with its own strengths, and a chapter that asks what a curve is *for* when the question is causal, @sec-causal-inference-splines.

Three things to remember. A curve across animals and a curve within animals are different models, even when the figure looks the same, and the design decides which one you have. The dependence between the days of an animal is an empirical question, and in these mice it was a trait of the animal and not a memory of the last session, which I found out by looking before I modeled. And a curve is good where the days were measured: the derived quantities (the day of the peak, the day of the return, the rate on a day) are the useful answers it gives, each with an interval, and the days between and after the measured ones are the model's opinion, not yours.
